claim: Asymmetrically dividing stem cells often show asymmetric behavior of the mother versus daughter centrosomes, whereby the self-renewing stem cell selectively inherits the mother or daughter centrosome.
source: Asymmetrically dividing stem cells often show asymmetric behavior of the mother versus daughter centrosomes, whereby the self-renewing stem cell selectively inherits the mother or daughter centrosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Conduit and Raff, 2010; Habib et al., 2013; Januschke et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009; Yamashita et al., 2007) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Alms1a is a Drosophila homolog of the human ciliopathy gene Alstrom syndrome.
source: Here, we show that Alms1a, a Drosophila homolog of the human ciliopathy gene Alstrom syndrome, is enriched on the mother centrosome in Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the abstract and is based on sequence homology analysis.

claim: Alms1a is enriched on the mother centrosome in Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs).
source: Here, we show that Alms1a, a Drosophila homolog of the human ciliopathy gene Alstrom syndrome, is enriched on the mother centrosome in Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2 and quantified in Figure 2K.

claim: Depletion of alms1a in GSCs results in rapid loss of centrosomes due to a failure in daughter centriole duplication.
source: Depletion of alms1a in GSCs, but not in differentiating germ cells, results in rapid loss of centrosomes due to a failure in daughter centriole duplication, suggesting that Alms1a has a stem-cell-specific function in centrosome duplication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3, including centrosome counts and centriole marker analysis.

claim: Alms1a has a stem-cell-specific function in centrosome duplication.
source: Depletion of alms1a in GSCs, but not in differentiating germ cells, results in rapid loss of centrosomes due to a failure in daughter centriole duplication, suggesting that Alms1a has a stem-cell-specific function in centrosome duplication.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing the effects of alms1a depletion in GSCs versus differentiating cells, as shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Alms1a interacts with Sak/Plk4, a critical regulator of centriole duplication.
source: Alms1a interacts with Sak/Plk4, a critical regulator of centriole duplication, more strongly at the GSC mother centrosome, further supporting Alms1a's unique role in GSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation, GST pulldown, bacterial two-hybrid, and BiFC experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Alms1a interacts more strongly with Sak/Plk4 at the GSC mother centrosome.
source: Alms1a interacts with Sak/Plk4, a critical regulator of centriole duplication, more strongly at the GSC mother centrosome, further supporting Alms1a's unique role in GSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC analysis shown in Figure 5F-L, which shows stronger interaction signal at GSC mother centrosomes.

claim: Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs) divide asymmetrically by orienting their spindle perpendicular toward the hub cells.
source: Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs) divide asymmetrically by orienting their spindle perpendicular toward the hub cells, the major niche component (Yamashita et al., 2003; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Yamashita et al., 2003) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: During male GSC divisions, the mother centrosome is always located near the hub-GSC junction.
source: During male GSC divisions, the mother centrosome is always located near the hub-GSC junction, whereas the daughter centrosome migrates to the other side of the cell, leading to spindle orientation perpendicular to the hub and consistent inheritance of the mother centrosome by GSCs (Figure 1A; Yamashita et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Yamashita et al., 2007) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The daughter centrosome migrates to the other side of the cell during male GSC divisions.
source: During male GSC divisions, the mother centrosome is always located near the hub-GSC junction, whereas the daughter centrosome migrates to the other side of the cell, leading to spindle orientation perpendicular to the hub and consistent inheritance of the mother centrosome by GSCs (Figure 1A; Yamashita et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Yamashita et al., 2007) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: GSCs consistently inherit the mother centrosome.
source: During male GSC divisions, the mother centrosome is always located near the hub-GSC junction, whereas the daughter centrosome migrates to the other side of the cell, leading to spindle orientation perpendicular to the hub and consistent inheritance of the mother centrosome by GSCs (Figure 1A; Yamashita et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Yamashita et al., 2007) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Klp10A is a microtubule-depolymerizing kinesin of kinesin-13 family.
source: Previously, we reported that Klp10A, a microtubule-depolymerizing kinesin of kinesin-13 family, is enriched on GSC centrosomes, but not on centrosomes of differentiating germ cells (i.e. gonialblasts (GBs) and spermatogonia (SGs)) (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016) and is based on established protein classification.

claim: Klp10A is enriched on GSC centrosomes, but not on centrosomes of differentiating germ cells.
source: Previously, we reported that Klp10A, a microtubule-depolymerizing kinesin of kinesin-13 family, is enriched on GSC centrosomes, but not on centrosomes of differentiating germ cells (i.e. gonialblasts (GBs) and spermatogonia (SGs)) (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016).

claim: Klp10A is the first protein reported to exhibit stem-cell-specific centrosome localization.
source: Klp10A is the first protein reported to exhibit stem-cell-specific centrosome localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016) and represents a priority claim.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of klp10A leads to abnormal elongation of the mother centrosomes in GSCs.
source: RNAi-mediated depletion of klp10A leads to abnormal elongation of the mother centrosomes in GSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016).

claim: The abnormally elongated mother centrosome in klp10A-depleted GSCs result in mitotic spindles with an asymmetric morphology.
source: The abnormally elongated mother centrosome in klp10A-depleted GSCs result in mitotic spindles with an asymmetric morphology (large vs. small half spindles) and the generation of a large GSC and a small GB that often dies, likely due to an insufficient cell size (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016).

claim: klp10A-depleted GSCs generate a large GSC and a small GB that often dies, likely due to an insufficient cell size.
source: The abnormally elongated mother centrosome in klp10A-depleted GSCs result in mitotic spindles with an asymmetric morphology (large vs. small half spindles) and the generation of a large GSC and a small GB that often dies, likely due to an insufficient cell size (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016) and includes a speculative explanation for cell death.

claim: GSC centrosomes are under unique regulation.
source: These results suggested that stem cell centrosomes are indeed under unique regulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of GSC-specific centrosomal proteins and their unique functions.

claim: Alms1a was identified as a candidate from Klp10A pulldown and mass spectrometry analysis.
source: Using this approach, we identified 260 candidates (Supplementary file 1), including two homologs of Alstrom syndrome (Alms) 1, a causal gene for a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by childhood obesity and sensory impairment, categorized as multiorgan ciliopathy (Marshall et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data described in the manuscript and referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The Drosophila genome encodes two Alms1 homologs, alms1a (CG12179) and alms1b (CG12184).
source: The Drosophila genome encodes two Alms1 homologs, juxtaposed to each other on the X chromosome, which we named alms1a (CG12179) and alms1b (CG12184).
evidence: This claim is based on genome annotation and sequence analysis.

claim: alms1a and alms1b are juxtaposed to each other on the X chromosome.
source: The Drosophila genome encodes two Alms1 homologs, juxtaposed to each other on the X chromosome, which we named alms1a (CG12179) and alms1b (CG12184).
evidence: This claim is based on genome annotation and sequence analysis.

claim: Alms1a localized to centrosomes in all germ cells (GSCs to spermatids).
source: We raised specific antibodies against Alms1a and Alms1b, and found that Alms1a localized to centrosomes in all germ cells (GSCs to spermatids) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), whereas Alms1b was not expressed until a late stage of spermatogenesis and localized to the basal body of elongating spermatids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alms1b was not expressed until a late stage of spermatogenesis and localized to the basal body of elongating spermatids.
source: We raised specific antibodies against Alms1a and Alms1b, and found that Alms1a localized to centrosomes in all germ cells (GSCs to spermatids) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), whereas Alms1b was not expressed until a late stage of spermatogenesis and localized to the basal body of elongating spermatids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Alms1a and Klp10A co-immunoprecipitated in GSC-enriched extract but not in SG-enriched extract.
source: Alms1a and Klp10A co-immunoprecipitated in GSC-enriched extract but not in SG-enriched extract, confirming that Alms1a is a GSC-specific Klp10A interactor (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The physical interaction between Alms1a and Klp10A is direct.
source: We found that this physical interaction between Alms1a and Klp10A is direct, and mediated via Alms1a's conserved C-terminal region ('ALMS motif'), as demonstrated by pulldown of the GST-fusion protein expressed in bacterial cells (Figure 1E–F) as well as by a bacterial two hybrid method (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown data (Figure 1E-F) and bacterial two-hybrid data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The interaction between Alms1a and Klp10A is mediated via Alms1a's conserved C-terminal region ('ALMS motif').
source: We found that this physical interaction between Alms1a and Klp10A is direct, and mediated via Alms1a's conserved C-terminal region ('ALMS motif'), as demonstrated by pulldown of the GST-fusion protein expressed in bacterial cells (Figure 1E–F) as well as by a bacterial two hybrid method (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown data (Figure 1E-F) and bacterial two-hybrid data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: BiFC signals between Alms1a and Klp10A were observed at centrosomes in GSCs, but not in the GB and SGs.
source: Upon co-expression of alms1a-VNm9 and VC155-klp10A in the germline (nos-gal4>UAS-alms1a-VNm9, UAS-VC155-klp10A), we observed a YFP signal at centrosomes in GSCs, but not in the GB and SGs (Figure 1G,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 1G,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The interaction between Alms1a and Klp10A is GSC-specific.
source: The lack of BiFC signals in the GB and SG serves as an internal negative control and confirms that the interaction between Alms1a and Klp10A is GSC-specific.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the BiFC data showing signals only in GSCs but not in GB and SGs.

claim: Alms1a is more enriched on the mother centrosome than the daughter centrosome in GSCs.
source: We found that, although Alms1a localized to centrosomes in all cell types, it was more enriched on the mother centrosome than the daughter centrosome in GSCs (Figure 2B–D,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B-D and quantified in Figure 2K.

claim: The two centrosomes in SGs had an equivalent amount of Alms1a.
source: In contrast, the two centrosomes in SGs had an equivalent amount of Alms1a (Figure 2E–G,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E-G and quantified in Figure 2K.

claim: klp10ARNAi did not affect Alms1a localization to the SG centrosomes.
source: klp10ARNAi did not affect Alms1a localization to the SG centrosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Germline knockdown of alms1a did not compromise Klp10A localization in GSCs.
source: Germline knockdown of alms1a (nos-gal4>alms1TRiP.HMJ30289, referred as to alms1RNAi hereafter) did not compromise Klp10A localization in GSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Alms1a localization to the centrosome mostly did not overlap with Centrobin (Cnb), a daughter centriole marker.
source: Alms1a localization to the centrosome mostly did not overlap with Centrobin (Cnb), a daughter centriole marker (Januschke et al., 2013; Figure 2B,D–G), suggesting that Alms1a might localize to the mother centriole (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B,D-G and a citation to published work (Januschke et al., 2013).

claim: Alms1a is a mother centriole protein in GSCs and GBs/SGs.
source: Detailed examination of Alms1a localization using Lightning confocal microscopy (see Materials and methods) confirmed that Alms1a is a mother centriole protein in GSCs and GBs/SGs (Figure 2L–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2L-N.

claim: Alms1a localizes to the proximal end of the mother centriole.
source: We found that Alms1a localizes to the proximal end of the mother centriole: it localizes to the Ana1-positive centriole (e.g. mother centriole) at the opposite end compared to CP110, which is at the distal end (Figure 2M,N).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2M,N using markers for proximal (Ana1) and distal (CP110) ends.

claim: Alms1a appeared to extend toward the proximal end of the daughter centriole specifically in the GSC mother centrosome.
source: In addition to this localization at the proximal end of the mother centriole, Alms1a appeared to extend toward the proximal end of the daughter centriole specifically in the GSC mother centrosome (Figure 2L).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Alms1a staining appears as two spots within the GSC mother centrosome.
source: We found that Alms1a staining appears as two spots within the GSC mother centrosome (Figure 2P), but as one spot within the GSC daughter centrosome and GB/SG centrosomes (Figure 2Q–R).
evidence: This claim is supported by STED super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2P.

claim: Alms1a staining appears as one spot within the GSC daughter centrosome and GB/SG centrosomes.
source: We found that Alms1a staining appears as two spots within the GSC mother centrosome (Figure 2P), but as one spot within the GSC daughter centrosome and GB/SG centrosomes (Figure 2Q–R).
evidence: This claim is supported by STED super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2Q-R.

claim: Alms1a localizes to the mother and daughter centrioles at the GSC mother centrosomes, but only to the mother centrioles elsewhere.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that Alms1a localizes to the mother and daughter centrioles at the GSC mother centrosomes, but only to the mother centrioles elsewhere, generating an asymmetry between mother vs. daughter centrosomes of GSCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined microscopy data showing differential Alms1a localization patterns.

claim: Knockdown of alms1a resulted in the complete loss of centrosomes from all germ cells, except for the mother centrosomes in GSCs.
source: Knockdown of alms1a (nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi, whereby RNAi is induced starting from embryogenesis) resulted in the complete loss of centrosomes from all germ cells, except for the mother centrosomes in GSCs, suggesting that alms1a is required for generating new centrosomes/centrioles (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: alms1a is required for generating new centrosomes/centrioles.
source: Knockdown of alms1a (nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi, whereby RNAi is induced starting from embryogenesis) resulted in the complete loss of centrosomes from all germ cells, except for the mother centrosomes in GSCs, suggesting that alms1a is required for generating new centrosomes/centrioles (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that alms1a depletion leads to centrosome loss.

claim: Many alms1RNAi GSCs contained only one centrosome (i.e. mother).
source: In contrast, many alms1RNAi GSCs contained only one centrosome (i.e. mother), visualized by Asl as well as γ-Tubulin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The remaining centrosome in alms1RNAi GSCs gradually elongated.
source: Interestingly, the remaining centrosome in alms1RNAi GSCs gradually elongated (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), similar to our earlier observation with klp10ARNAi (Chen et al., 2016): in klp10ARNAi GSCs, the mother centrosome gradually elongated, whereas the daughter centrosome was slightly smaller than normal, although it was not lost as is observed in alms1RNAi GSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: klp10A and alms1a share a similar function, possibly balancing the growth of mother vs. daughter centrosomes.
source: These data suggest that klp10A and alms1a share a similar function, possibly balancing the growth of mother vs. daughter centrosomes (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the similar phenotypes of klp10A and alms1a depletion.

claim: alms1a is required for centrosome duplication in GSCs.
source: We conclude that alms1a is required for centrosome duplication in GSCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that alms1a depletion leads to loss of daughter centrosomes in GSCs.

claim: GSCs lose their daughter centrosomes as fast as 1–2 days (2–4 GSC cell cycles) upon RNAi-mediated knockdown of alms1a.
source: This approach confirmed that GSCs lose their daughter centrosomes as fast as 1–2 days (2–4 GSC cell cycles) upon RNAi-mediated knockdown of alms1a (Figure 3E), and allowed us to examine the process of centrosome loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Upon knockdown of alms1a, Cnb is lost or diminished from the mother centrosome prior to centrosome loss.
source: However, upon knockdown of alms1a, Cnb is lost or diminished from the mother centrosome prior to centrosome loss: when GSCs still contained two γ-Tubulin-positive centrosomes, the mother centrosome lacked Cnb staining, suggesting that it does not contain the daughter centriole (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Centriole duplication is compromised in GSCs upon alms1 depletion.
source: Based on these results, we infer that centriole duplication is compromised in GSCs upon alms1 depletion: mother centriole (lacking Cnb) and daughter centriole (marked by Cnb) of the GSC mother centrosome likely split from each other, and segregate into GSC and GB, respectively, without duplicating centrioles (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Cnb staining data and illustrated in Figure 3L.

claim: alms1RNAi GSCs contained only one centrosome, which contains only one centriole.
source: In contrast to control GSCs, which contain two centrosomes, each of which contains two centrioles marked by Cp110 (Figure 3I,K), alms1RNAi GSCs contained only one centrosome, which contains only one centriole (Figure 3J,K), demonstrating that alms1RNAi compromises centriole duplication.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3J,K.

claim: alms1RNAi compromises centriole duplication.
source: In contrast to control GSCs, which contain two centrosomes, each of which contains two centrioles marked by Cp110 (Figure 3I,K), alms1RNAi GSCs contained only one centrosome, which contains only one centriole (Figure 3J,K), demonstrating that alms1RNAi compromises centriole duplication.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced centriole numbers in alms1RNAi GSCs.

claim: nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies were sterile.
source: nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies were sterile, likely due to the complete loss of centrosomes, although knockdown of alms1b also contributes to this sterility (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by fertility assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: alms1a plays a critical role in ensuring centrosome duplication in GSCs, which is essential for the production of centrosomes/centrioles in all downstream germ cells.
source: Taken together, we conclude that alms1a plays a critical role in ensuring centrosome duplication in GSCs, which is essential for the production of centrosomes/centrioles in all downstream germ cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that alms1a depletion in GSCs leads to centrosome loss in all germ cells.

claim: SGs maintained their centrosomes upon depletion of alms1a.
source: We found that SGs, which divide symmetrically, maintained their centrosomes upon depletion of alms1a (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: alms1a is specifically required for centriole duplication in stem cells, but not in symmetrically dividing, differentiating cells.
source: Thus, alms1a is specifically required for centriole duplication in stem cells, but not in symmetrically dividing, differentiating cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of alms1a depletion in GSCs versus SGs.

claim: Symmetrically dividing GSCs retained their centrosomes upon alms1a depletion.
source: Importantly, these symmetrically dividing GSCs retained their centrosomes (Figure 4C–D), suggesting that alms1a is required for centriole duplication only in asymmetrically dividing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: alms1a is required for centriole duplication only in asymmetrically dividing cells.
source: Importantly, these symmetrically dividing GSCs retained their centrosomes (Figure 4C–D), suggesting that alms1a is required for centriole duplication only in asymmetrically dividing cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that symmetrically dividing GSCs do not require alms1a for centrosome maintenance.

claim: Alms1a physically interacted with Sak and Sas-6 in testes lysates enriched with GSCs.
source: Alms1a physically interacted with Sak and Sas-6 in testes lysates enriched with GSCs, as indicated by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Sak directly binds to Alms1a via the ALMS motif.
source: Moreover, GST-pulldown experiments using bacterial extracts as well as bacterial two hybrid experiments showed that Sak directly binds to Alms1a via the ALMS motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown and bacterial two-hybrid data shown in Figure 5C-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sas-6-ALMS motif did not interact in bacterial extract.
source: In contrast, Sas-6-ALMS motif did not interact in bacterial extract (Figure 5C–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the interaction between Alms1a and Sas-6 in testis extract is indirect.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown and bacterial two-hybrid data shown in Figure 5C-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction between Alms1a and Sas-6 in testis extract is indirect.
source: In contrast, Sas-6-ALMS motif did not interact in bacterial extract (Figure 5C–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the interaction between Alms1a and Sas-6 in testis extract is indirect.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of direct interaction in bacterial extracts despite co-immunoprecipitation in testis lysates.

claim: The BiFC signal between Alms1a and Sak was significantly higher at the GSC mother centrosome.
source: We observed a weak BiFC signal at centrosomes in general, but the BiFC signal was significantly higher at the GSC mother centrosome (Figure 5F–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 5F-L.

claim: The Alms1a-Sak interaction preferentially occurs at the daughter centriole of the GSC mother centrosome.
source: Given that Alms1a localizes to the mother centriole in all centrosomes, but to the daughter centriole only in GSCs (Figure 2), we infer that the Alms1a-Sak interaction preferentially occurs at the daughter centriole of the GSC mother centrosome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the BiFC data and the known localization pattern of Alms1a.

claim: Overexpression of alms1a alone did not result in an obvious increase in centrosome number compared to the control.
source: Overexpression of alms1a (nos-gal4 >UAS-alms1a-GFP, 25°C) alone did not result in an obvious increase in centrosome number compared to the control (2.09 ± 0.38 centrosomes/cell in alms1a overexpression, vs. 2.00 ± 0.00 centrosomes/cell in control) (Figure 6A,B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by centrosome counting data shown in Figure 6A,B,E.

claim: Sak overexpression increased centrosome numbers slightly.
source: Sak overexpression increased centrosome numbers slightly (2.79 ± 1.07 centrosomes/cell) (Figure 6C,E), similar to observations in other cell types (Habedanck et al., 2005; Peel et al., 2007; Rodrigues-Martins et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by centrosome counting data shown in Figure 6C,E and citations to published work.

claim: Co-expression of alms1a and sak dramatically enhanced centrosome overduplication.
source: Strikingly, co-expression of alms1a and sak (nos-gal4>UAS-alms1a-GFP, UAS-GFP-sak, 25°C) dramatically enhanced centrosome overduplication (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (4.61 ± 1.91 centrosomes/cell).
evidence: This claim is supported by centrosome counting data shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alms1a promotes centrosome duplication together with Sak, possibly by recruiting Sak to the site of centriole duplication in GSCs.
source: These results suggest that Alms1a promotes centrosome duplication together with Sak, possibly by recruiting Sak to the site of centriole duplication in GSCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the synergistic effect of alms1a and sak co-expression on centrosome overduplication.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of alms1a in GSCs resulted in the excessive enrichment of both Sak and Sas-6 at the elongated mother centriole.
source: Interestingly, we found that RNAi-mediated knockdown of alms1a in GSCs resulted in the excessive enrichment of both Sak and Sas-6 at the elongated mother centriole that remains after all other centrosomes are depleted (Figure 6F–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6F-K.

claim: The excess amount of Sak and Sas-6 on the remaining mother centriole in alms1RNAi GSCs may explain why it continues to elongate.
source: The excess amount of Sak and Sas-6 on the remaining mother centriole in alms1RNAi GSCs may explain why it continues to elongate.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation of excessive Sak and Sas-6 accumulation and centriole elongation.

claim: The accumulation of Sak and Sas-6 on the mother centriole may deplete Sak and Sas-6 from the site of the daughter centriole production, leading to the failure in daughter centriole duplication.
source: In parallel, the accumulation of Sak and Sas-6 on the mother centriole may deplete Sak and Sas-6 from the site of the daughter centriole production, leading to the failure in daughter centriole duplication.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the observed failure in daughter centriole duplication.

claim: The GSC-specific function of Alms1a may be to promote daughter centriole duplication by recruiting Sak to the 'seeding site' for daughter centriole duplication.
source: Therefore, the GSC-specific function of Alms1a may be to promote daughter centriole duplication by recruiting Sak to the 'seeding site' for daughter centriole duplication (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a model for Alms1a function based on the observed data.

claim: Human ALMS1 is reported to localize to the centrosome/basal body in many cells and function in formation/maintenance of the cilia.
source: Human ALMS1 is reported to localize to the centrosome/basal body in many cells and function in formation/maintenance of the cilia (Andersen et al., 2003; Hearn et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Andersen et al., 2003; Hearn et al., 2005).

claim: Alstrom syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by childhood obesity and sensory impairment, categorized as multiorgan ciliopathy.
source: Using this approach, we identified 260 candidates (Supplementary file 1), including two homologs of Alstrom syndrome (Alms) 1, a causal gene for a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by childhood obesity and sensory impairment, categorized as multiorgan ciliopathy (Marshall et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Marshall et al., 2011) and represents established medical knowledge.

claim: The specific requirement of alms1a only in asymmetrically dividing adult stem cells may partly explain the reported late-onset nature of Alstrom syndrome.
source: This specific requirement of alms1a only in a subset of cell types (e.g. asymmetrically dividing adult stem cells) may partly explain the reported late-onset nature of Alstrom syndrome, which exhibits symptoms progressively during childhood, as opposed to many other ciliopathies that are associated with disease symptoms at birth (Braun and Hildebrandt, 2017).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a connection between the cell-type-specific function of alms1a and the clinical presentation of Alstrom syndrome, supported by a citation (Braun and Hildebrandt, 2017).

claim: Alms1a may promote daughter centriole duplication by recruiting Sak (and Sas-6), to the daughter centriole of the GSC mother centrosome.
source: Therefore, we postulate that Alms1a may promote daughter centriole duplication by recruiting Sak (and Sas-6), to the daughter centriole of the GSC mother centrosome.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a model for Alms1a function based on the observed interactions and localization patterns.

claim: Alms1a is required to 'discourage' mother centriole's growth and 'encourage' daughter centrioles generation/growth.
source: Given that alms1RNAi leads to excessive overgrowth of mother centriole of the GSC mother centrosome at the expense of the daughter centriole duplication, it is tempting to speculate that Alms1a is required to 'discourage' mother centriole's growth and 'encourage' daughter centrioles generation/growth.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a model for Alms1a function based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: The mother centriole of the mother centrosome in GSCs may have a stronger microtubule nucleation activity, which may interfere with production of new centrioles.
source: Perhaps to ensure correct centrosome positioning, the mother centriole of the mother centrosome in GSCs may have a stronger microtubule nucleation activity, which may interfere with production of new centrioles.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism to explain the unique requirement for Alms1a in GSCs.

claim: Ninein specifically localizes to the daughter centrosome when overexpressed in Drosophila neuroblasts and male GSCs.
source: A recent study identified Ninein as a protein that specifically localizes to the daughter centrosome when overexpressed in Drosophila neuroblasts and male GSCs (Zheng et al., 2016), although no phenotypic consequences were detected upon its depletion, leaving the role of its asymmetric localization unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Zheng et al., 2016).

claim: No phenotypic consequences were detected upon Ninein depletion.
source: A recent study identified Ninein as a protein that specifically localizes to the daughter centrosome when overexpressed in Drosophila neuroblasts and male GSCs (Zheng et al., 2016), although no phenotypic consequences were detected upon its depletion, leaving the role of its asymmetric localization unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Zheng et al., 2016).

claim: The Klp10A pull down did not identify Ninein.
source: Our Klp10A pull down did not identify Ninein, it will be of interest to study how Klp10A and Alms1a may be functionally related to Ninein.
evidence: This claim is based on the mass spectrometry data from the Klp10A pulldown experiment.

claim: GSC centrosomes are under unique regulation, involving GSC centrosome-specific proteins Klp10A and Alms1a.
source: Our study revealed that GSC centrosomes are indeed under unique regulation, involving GSC centrosome-specific proteins Klp10A and Alms1a.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the identification and characterization of GSC-specific centrosomal proteins and their functions.

claim: Expression of the full-length Alms1a rescued the centrosome loss phenotype of alms1RNAi phenotype partially.
source: Expression of the full-length Alms1a (nos-gal4>alms1a-GFP, made to be insensitive to RNAi, see Materials and methods) rescued the centrosome loss phenotype of alms1RNAi phenotype partially, suggesting that the phenotype is caused, at least in part, by the loss of alms1a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phenotype of alms1RNAi is caused, at least in part, by the loss of alms1a.
source: Expression of the full-length Alms1a (nos-gal4>alms1a-GFP, made to be insensitive to RNAi, see Materials and methods) rescued the centrosome loss phenotype of alms1RNAi phenotype partially, suggesting that the phenotype is caused, at least in part, by the loss of alms1a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the partial rescue of the phenotype by alms1a expression.

claim: Wild-type GSCs normally contain mother and daughter centrosomes, each of which contains both mother and daughter centrioles, throughout the cell cycle.
source: Wild-type GSCs normally contain mother and daughter centrosomes, each of which contains both mother and daughter centrioles, throughout the cell cycle, due to early duplication of the centrosome right after the previous mitosis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of centrosome structure and cell cycle, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: Centrosome duplication in GSCs occurs early, right after the previous mitosis.
source: Wild-type GSCs normally contain mother and daughter centrosomes, each of which contains both mother and daughter centrioles, throughout the cell cycle, due to early duplication of the centrosome right after the previous mitosis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of centrosome duplication timing in the cell cycle.

claim: In klp10ARNAi GSCs, the mother centrosome gradually elongated, whereas the daughter centrosome was slightly smaller than normal.
source: Interestingly, the remaining centrosome in alms1RNAi GSCs gradually elongated (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), similar to our earlier observation with klp10ARNAi (Chen et al., 2016): in klp10ARNAi GSCs, the mother centrosome gradually elongated, whereas the daughter centrosome was slightly smaller than normal, although it was not lost as is observed in alms1RNAi GSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016).

claim: The daughter centrosome in klp10ARNAi GSCs was not lost, unlike in alms1RNAi GSCs.
source: Interestingly, the remaining centrosome in alms1RNAi GSCs gradually elongated (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), similar to our earlier observation with klp10ARNAi (Chen et al., 2016): in klp10ARNAi GSCs, the mother centrosome gradually elongated, whereas the daughter centrosome was slightly smaller than normal, although it was not lost as is observed in alms1RNAi GSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Chen et al., 2016) and comparison with alms1RNAi phenotype.

claim: Mother centriole and daughter centriole of the GSC mother centrosome likely split from each other, and segregate into GSC and GB, respectively, without duplicating centrioles in alms1-depleted GSCs.
source: Based on these results, we infer that centriole duplication is compromised in GSCs upon alms1 depletion: mother centriole (lacking Cnb) and daughter centriole (marked by Cnb) of the GSC mother centrosome likely split from each other, and segregate into GSC and GB, respectively, without duplicating centrioles (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Cnb staining data and illustrated in Figure 3L.

claim: In the following cell cycle after alms1 depletion, the GSCs that are incapable of duplicating centrioles will continue to divide without passing any new centrosomes to GBs.
source: In the following cell cycle, the GSCs that are incapable of duplicating centrioles will continue to divide without passing any new centrosomes to GBs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the model of centriole duplication failure in alms1-depleted GSCs.

claim: The lack of centriole duplication in GSCs would lead to loss of centrosomes/centrioles in all germ cells.
source: The lack of centriole duplication in GSCs would lead to loss of centrosomes/centrioles in all germ cells, which must inherit the first template for centriole duplication from GSCs (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the model illustrated in Figure 3L.

claim: All germ cells must inherit the first template for centriole duplication from GSCs.
source: The lack of centriole duplication in GSCs would lead to loss of centrosomes/centrioles in all germ cells, which must inherit the first template for centriole duplication from GSCs (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of germline development and centriole inheritance.

claim: The sterility of nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies is likely due to the complete loss of centrosomes.
source: nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies were sterile, likely due to the complete loss of centrosomes, although knockdown of alms1b also contributes to this sterility (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed centrosome loss phenotype and sterility.

claim: Knockdown of alms1b contributes to the sterility of nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies.
source: nos-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies were sterile, likely due to the complete loss of centrosomes, although knockdown of alms1b also contributes to this sterility (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fact that the RNAi construct targets both alms1a and alms1b.

claim: Alms1a was undetectable in SGs in the testis from bam-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies.
source: Note that this result was not due to incomplete depletion of alms1a, as Alms1a was undetectable in SGs in the testis from bam-gal4>UAS-alms1RNAi flies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Alms1a protein was undetectable in symmetrically dividing GSCs induced by upd expression together with alms1RNAi.
source: Alms1a protein was undetectable under this condition, confirming efficient knockdown (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Sak is a homolog of the Plk4 kinase, a master regulator required for centriole duplication.
source: Sak is a homolog of the Plk4 kinase, a master regulator required for centriole duplication (Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2005; Habedanck et al., 2005), whereas Sas-6 is a component for cartwheel assembly to promote centriole formation (Nakazawa et al., 2007; Rodrigues-Martins et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2005; Habedanck et al., 2005) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Sas-6 is a component for cartwheel assembly to promote centriole formation.
source: Sak is a homolog of the Plk4 kinase, a master regulator required for centriole duplication (Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2005; Habedanck et al., 2005), whereas Sas-6 is a component for cartwheel assembly to promote centriole formation (Nakazawa et al., 2007; Rodrigues-Martins et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Nakazawa et al., 2007; Rodrigues-Martins et al., 2007a) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Ana1 is a core centriole protein required for centrosome assembly.
source: Ana1 is a core centriole protein required for centrosome assembly and is known to localize to the mother centriole in early interphase (Fu et al., 2016; Goshima et al., 2007), whereas Cp110 localizes to the distal end of both mother and daughter centrioles, where it 'caps' the centriole (Delgehyr et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Fu et al., 2016; Goshima et al., 2007) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Ana1 is known to localize to the mother centriole in early interphase.
source: Ana1 is a core centriole protein required for centrosome assembly and is known to localize to the mother centriole in early interphase (Fu et al., 2016; Goshima et al., 2007), whereas Cp110 localizes to the distal end of both mother and daughter centrioles, where it 'caps' the centriole (Delgehyr et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Fu et al., 2016; Goshima et al., 2007) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Cp110 localizes to the distal end of both mother and daughter centrioles, where it 'caps' the centriole.
source: Ana1 is a core centriole protein required for centrosome assembly and is known to localize to the mother centriole in early interphase (Fu et al., 2016; Goshima et al., 2007), whereas Cp110 localizes to the distal end of both mother and daughter centrioles, where it 'caps' the centriole (Delgehyr et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Delgehyr et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2009) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Klp10A exhibits pan centrosomal (broadly pericentrosomal) localization in GSCs.
source: It should be noted that, although Klp10A was reported to be more concentrated at the distal end of the centriole in Drosophila spermatocytes (Delgehyr et al., 2012; Riparbelli et al., 2018), Klp10A exhibits pan centrosomal (broadly pericentrosomal) localization in GSCs (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Chen et al., 2016; Delgehyr et al., 2012; Riparbelli et al., 2018).

claim: Klp10A-Alms1a interaction likely occurs at the proximal end of the centrioles, where Alms1a is most concentrated.
source: We suggest that Klp10A-Alms1a interaction likely occurs at the proximal end of the centrioles, where Alms1a is most concentrated, although other possibilities as to the site of their functional interaction cannot be excluded.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the localization patterns of Klp10A and Alms1a, but acknowledges uncertainty.

claim: The mammalian Alms1 protein was previously shown to localize to centrosomes and basal bodies of the primary cilia.
source: The mammalian Alms1 protein was previously shown to localize to centrosomes and basal bodies of the primary cilia (Andersen et al., 2003; Hearn et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Andersen et al., 2003; Hearn et al., 2005).

claim: The peptide sequences identified by mass-spectrometry analysis were identical between alms1a and alms1b.
source: The peptide sequences identified by our mass-spectrometry analysis were identical between these two proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on the mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: Alms1a is likely the relevant Klp10A interactor in GSCs.
source: Therefore, Alms1a is likely the relevant Klp10A interactor in GSCs: accordingly, we focused on Alms1a in this study.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression and localization patterns of Alms1a and Alms1b.

claim: Centrobin (Cnb) is a daughter centriole marker.
source: Alms1a localization to the centrosome mostly did not overlap with Centrobin (Cnb), a daughter centriole marker (Januschke et al., 2013; Figure 2B,D–G), suggesting that Alms1a might localize to the mother centriole (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work (Januschke et al., 2013) and represents established knowledge.

claim: The Asl ring observed in GSC centrosomes matches to the dimension of the Asl ring reported in other Drosophila cells.
source: To achieve better resolution, we used stimulated emission depletion (STED) super-resolution microscopy: the mother centriole was marked by Asl, which is known to surround the mother centriole in a ring shape (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The Asl ring observed in GSC centrosomes matches to the dimension of the Asl ring reported in other Drosophila cells (Fu et al., 2016; Galletta et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Fu et al., 2016; Galletta et al., 2016) and comparison with the current data.

claim: Asl is known to surround the mother centriole in a ring shape.
source: To achieve better resolution, we used stimulated emission depletion (STED) super-resolution microscopy: the mother centriole was marked by Asl, which is known to surround the mother centriole in a ring shape (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Asl localization.
